howTo.title: How to make one
items: Pick the template closest to your day (elementary, middle/high school, exam prep, college or office worker) and the circular chart fills in right away.
Edit names and start/end times in the list and the chart updates instantly. Times use 10-minute steps; if the end is earlier than the start (23:00–07:00) the activity runs past midnight.
Tap the color square to change its color. Duplicate adds an activity of the same length right after, handy for alternating study and breaks.
Overlapping activities trigger a yellow notice, and time with no activity shows up as Unplanned in the totals.
Add a title and your goal, then save a PNG or print one A4 page for your desk. Copy link sends the exact schedule to parents or friends.

tips.title: Tips for a schedule that sticks
items: Set bedtime and wake-up time first. Keeping your vacation wake-up time close to your school-day one makes the return to school easier.
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) recommends 9–12 hours of sleep for ages 6–12, 8–10 hours for ages 13–18, and 7 or more hours for adults. The templates keep sleep within these ranges.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for ages 5–17, and 150–300 minutes a week of moderate activity for adults. Add an exercise slot at least once a day.
Split long study sessions and put breaks in between. Naming the slot after the task (e.g. Math workbook) makes it easier to follow through.
Plan free time too. Start with what you can actually keep, try it for a week, then adjust it to the times you really kept.

items.q: How do I make a daily schedule?
items.a: Pick a template close to your day, then edit names and start/end times in the list; the circular schedule updates instantly. Add a title and goal and choose Save image or Print. It is free, with no sign-up or install.

items.q: What should a vacation schedule include?
items.a: Put in daily routines first (sleep, meals, washing up), then homework, study or classes, exercise, reading and free time. Daily time totals shows whether all 24 hours are filled.

items.q: How much sleep do elementary and teenage students need?
items.a: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) recommends 9–12 hours a day for ages 6–12 and 8–10 hours for ages 13–18. The elementary template uses 21:30–07:30 (10 hours) and the middle/high school template 23:30–07:30 (8 hours).

items.q: How do I enter something that runs past midnight, like 11 pm to 7 am?
items.a: Set the start to 23:00 and the end to 07:00; it counts as one activity crossing midnight and is drawn as a single slice passing 0 o'clock.

items.q: What happens if activities overlap or leave gaps?
items.a: A yellow notice above the list shows which activities overlap and by how many minutes. Time with no activity stays gray on the chart and appears as Unplanned in the totals.

items.q: Can I print the schedule or save it as an image?
items.a: Save image downloads a PNG with the title, the circular chart and your goal. Print fits just the schedule on one portrait A4 page, and the print dialog can also save it as a PDF.

Every change is saved automatically in this browser, so you can pick up where you left off. Nothing is sent to a server. To view it on another device or send it to someone, copy the link; opening it shows the same schedule.

items.q: Can exam-prep students or office workers use it?
items.a: Yes. The exam-prep template has 12 hours of study and 7 hours of sleep, and the office worker weekday template has 8 hours of work and 2 hours of commuting. For weekends or shift work, just edit the times and names in the list.
